name: Irene Doukaina
title: Augusta, wife of Alexios I Komnenos
roles: Empress consort of Alexios I Komnenos
Mother of John II Komnenos and Anna Komnene

imageInfo.caption: An enamel on the Pala d'Oro in Saint Mark's, Venice, inscribed “Irene, most pious Augusta” and generally identified as Irene Doukaina.
imageInfo.creator: Unknown Byzantine enameller
imageInfo.note: Probably made in her lifetime, but a formal enamel type with no individual features; the inscription gives only the name Irene, so the identification rests on the altarpiece's twelfth-century history.

summary: Doukas heiress married at about twelve to Alexios I Komnenos, whose family backing helped him to the throne in 1081; mother of Anna Komnene and John II Komnenos, she grew powerful late in the reign and failed to put Anna's husband on the throne in 1118.
overview: Irene Doukaina brought the support of the Doukas family to Alexios I Komnenos and was nearly set aside once he had the throne. Overshadowed for twenty years by her mother-in-law Anna Dalassene, she became her husband's companion on campaign and his deputy in his last years, then tried in vain to make her daughter Anna Komnene's husband emperor in place of her son John II Komnenos.
greatestFeats: Crowned empress in 1081 despite efforts to exclude her
Took charge of the civil government for the ailing Alexios I Komnenos in his last years
Founded the convent of the Theotokos Kecharitomene in Constantinople
Patron of writers, including Nikephoros Bryennios, Theophylact of Ohrid and Michael Italikos

birth.note: Born to Andronikos Doukas and Maria, a granddaughter of the Bulgarian tsar Ivan Vladislav.

death.circumstance: Died in retirement after 1118; the day is recorded but the year is disputed, and some works give 1138.

quickFacts.knownFor: The Doukas marriage behind the Komnenian dynasty and the failed succession plot of 1118

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Irene Doukaina was empress of the Byzantine Empire from 1081 to 1118 as the wife of Alexios I Komnenos. A great-niece of Constantine X Doukas, she married Alexios in 1078, and the backing of her family was essential when he seized Constantinople in 1081. His mother, Anna Dalassene, an old enemy of the Doukas family, wanted her replaced, and she was crowned a week after her husband only because her relatives insisted.

For twenty years Anna Dalassene ran the palace while the young empress stayed in her shadow. After her mother-in-law retired, she became Alexios's constant companion, travelling with him on campaign and taking over the civil administration when he was ill. Her daughter Anna Komnene idolised her in the Alexiad; the historian Niketas Choniates remembered her instead as the mother who tried to disinherit her own son, John II Komnenos, in favour of Anna and her husband Nikephoros Bryennios.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Irene Doukaina was born around 1066. Her father, Andronikos Doukas, was the elder son of the Caesar John Doukas, brother of Constantine X Doukas, and her mother, Maria, was a granddaughter of the Bulgarian tsar Ivan Vladislav. Her grandfather the Caesar was the most powerful figure at court in the 1070s. In 1078, when she was about twelve, she married the young general Alexios Komnenos, a match that tied the ambitious Komnenos brothers to the Doukas family in the year Michael VII Doukas lost his throne to Nikephoros III Botaneiates.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Anna Komnene's Alexiad gives her mother one of the most elaborate portraits in Byzantine literature: upright as a young sapling and perfectly proportioned, with light-blue eyes whose gaze both charmed and frightened, so beautiful that she might be called Athena made visible. Anna also describes a reserved woman who disliked appearing in public, read the lives of the saints, gave generously to monks and beggars, and nursed Alexios through his gout. This is a daughter's tribute, written in the convent where Anna shared her mother's disgrace, and it passes over anything that might embarrass either of them, including the rumours that Alexios had an affair with Maria of Alania early in the reign.

Other evidence shows a more determined figure. Anna says Alexios took the empress on campaign partly so that she could watch for plots against him, and some modern historians read this as a sign that he did not trust her alone in the capital. Niketas Choniates, writing two generations later, describes her nagging Alexios to name Bryennios as heir and mocking John as rash, pleasure-loving and weak, while the emperor pretended to be busy or lost his temper. Choniates liked to dramatise palace quarrels, but her attempt to pass over John in 1118 is not in doubt. Her reputation as a plotter lasted: the modern poet Constantine Cavafy called her a viper.

contentSections.title: A contested coronation
paragraphs: In the spring of 1081 Alexios and his brother Isaac rebelled against Nikephoros III Botaneiates, and the Doukas family, led by the Caesar John, gave them decisive support. Alexios entered Constantinople on 1 April and was crowned within days, but his wife was left out of the ceremony. Anna Dalassene is said to have wanted her son to divorce his young wife and marry Maria of Alania, the former wife of both Michael VII and Nikephoros III, who was still living in the palace. The Doukas family persuaded the patriarch Kosmas to crown her about a week later. Anna Dalassene accepted the coronation but forced Kosmas to resign and replaced him with her own candidate, Eustratios Garidas.
Her first child, Anna Komnene, was born on 1 December 1083, and her eldest son, John, on 13 September 1087. She bore nine children in all.

contentSections.title: Empress of Alexios I
paragraphs: For most of the reign the empress had little power. In 1081 Alexios gave his mother formal authority over the civil administration, and Anna Dalassene dominated the palace until she retired to a convent around 1100. Her position rose after that. She went with Alexios on campaign, including the war against Bohemond I of Antioch in 1107–1108 and the expedition to the Chersonese in 1112, and when she stayed in Constantinople she governed with Nikephoros Bryennios as her counsellor. Around 1112, when rheumatism left Alexios barely able to move, he handed her the civil government and control of access to him.

She used her wealth for religious foundations and learning. The convent of the Theotokos Kecharitomene, which she founded in Constantinople in the early twelfth century, has a surviving foundation charter, or typikon, which sets out its rules and makes provision for her daughters to live there. Anna Komnene says that it was at the empress's request that Nikephoros Bryennios began his history of Alexios's rise, and the empress also corresponded with Theophylact of Ohrid and supported Michael Italikos.

contentSections.title: The succession of 1118
paragraphs: Irene Doukaina wanted the throne to go to Anna and Bryennios rather than to John, who had been crowned co-emperor as a child in 1092. Alexios refused. As he lay dying in August 1118 she nursed him while still pressing her son-in-law's claim, and when John took his father's signet ring and hurried to secure the Great Palace, she accused him of theft and treachery. Alexios died on 15 August 1118. She mourned him deeply, but soon joined Anna in a conspiracy against John. Bryennios would not act, the plot failed, and mother and daughter withdrew to the Kecharitomene. It was a comfortable retirement: there she distributed food to the poor and paid for the upbringing and education of orphan girls.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Irene Doukaina died on 19 February, but the year is uncertain: modern works give 1123 or 1133, and some give 1138. The difference decides whether she lived five, fifteen or twenty years into the reign of the son she had tried to disinherit. She would have been in her late fifties at the earliest date and about seventy at the latest.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Her marriage joined the two families that dominated the empire for the next century, and later rulers used both names with pride: through one of her daughters she was the great-grandmother of the emperors Isaac II Angelos and Alexios III Angelos, and the founders of the Despotate of Epirus called themselves Komnenos Doukas. Anna Komnene's description of her is among the fullest portraits of a Byzantine woman to survive, and the Kecharitomene typikon is a major source for the lives of aristocratic nuns in twelfth-century Constantinople.
